strengths: The paper targets a meaningful and relatively underexplored fine-grained visual reasoning setting: route planning from high-resolution transit maps. This is a useful stress test for MLLMs because it combines OCR, symbol/line following, spatial connectivity, transfer reasoning, and strict structured output.

REASON MAP is reasonably well motivated and includes nontrivial curation: 30 cities across 13 countries, 1,008 human-verified QA pairs, multiple languages, route references from map services, and separate map/question difficulty labels.

The experimental section is informative, covering 15 MLLMs across open/closed and base/reasoning variants. The reported results reveal interesting behavior, especially the weak performance of open-source reasoning models and the large remaining gap even for strong closed-source systems.
The text-only ablation is a valuable diagnostic showing that some performance can come from priors rather than visual grounding, while stronger models benefit more clearly from visual input.
The paper is generally clear, with dataset construction, templates, evaluation algorithms, error cases, and limitations described in enough detail to understand the benchmark design.
weaknesses: The benchmark is useful, but the scientific conclusions are stronger than the evidence supports. Claims about reasoning models versus base models are confounded by model family, scale, proprietary preprocessing, API behavior, token limits, and unknown closed-source training differences. The paper acknowledges some unfairness but still frames the pattern as a central finding.

The evaluation metrics are somewhat ad hoc and under-validated. The correctness metric checks endpoints, route names, station membership, and transfer consistency, but does not clearly establish optimality despite prompts asking for an optimal route. The map score uses hand-designed weights and bonuses without correlation to human judgments or sensitivity analysis.

Difficulty-aware weighting is not well justified empirically, and some difficulty buckets are extremely small, e.g. only one sample for hard-middle and seven for hard-easy. This makes difficulty-level plots and conclusions unstable.
The dataset scale is modest for a benchmark paper, especially the 312-sample test set. Hard cases are a small minority, although they are arguably the most relevant for fine-grained visual reasoning.
The visual-input ablation is only run on a subset of models, limiting its ability to support broad claims about visual grounding across the evaluated systems.

Reproducibility has unresolved concerns. The paper says map images are not redistributed and relies on public sources and APIs; if exact map versions, preprocessing, annotations, and API-returned routes are not fully released, reproducing the dataset and reference answers may be difficult.

The comparison to existing benchmarks is helpful but slightly overstated: the novelty is mainly the transit-map domain and high-resolution route reasoning, not a fundamentally new evaluation paradigm.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence in exact implementation details, including unclear or malformed formulas in Algorithm 2, inconsistent terminology such as middle/medium, and extracted table/source links that are not fully informative in the manuscript text.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and underexplored evaluation setting: fine-grained visual reasoning over high-resolution transit maps, which are dense structured visual artifacts and meaningfully different from many existing diagram or VQA benchmarks.

REASONMAP includes useful benchmark ingredients: 30 cities across 13 countries, multilingual stop names, short and long route-planning questions, difficulty labels, a semi-automated construction pipeline, and human checking of route QA pairs.

The evaluation covers a reasonably broad set of 15 contemporary MLLMs, including open-source and closed-source base/reasoning variants, and reports both full-input and text-only settings to probe reliance on visual information.

The paper includes qualitative error analysis that surfaces concrete failure modes such as visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, and refusals, which helps interpret the benchmark beyond aggregate scores.
weaknesses: The benchmark is quite small for the strength of the claims: only 1,008 QA pairs are constructed and only 312 samples from 11 cities are used for the main test set. Some difficulty buckets are extremely sparse, including a bucket with one sample, making difficulty-wise conclusions unstable.

The main claims about base versus reasoning models are not well supported causally. The compared models differ in architecture, size, training data, API behavior, decoding constraints, and output-token budgets. The paper itself acknowledges closed-source comparisons are not fair, yet still draws broad conclusions about reasoning variants outperforming or underperforming base models.

The evaluation metrics are ad hoc and insufficiently validated. The proposed map score uses hand-chosen weights, caps, bonuses, and difficulty weights without sensitivity analysis or correlation with human judgments. Algorithm 2 is also ambiguously written, including expressions such as adding bonuses via “map_score + 10/map_score + 20” and a confusing normalization line, which raises concerns about reproducibility and implementation correctness.

Correctness and quality are confounded by strict output formatting. Several reported failures are format errors even when route information may be present, so the benchmark partly measures instruction-format compliance rather than visual route reasoning. This is especially consequential because invalid parses receive zero score.

Ground-truth construction depends on Google/Gaode route APIs plus manual filtering, but the manuscript provides limited detail on annotator procedures, inter-annotator agreement, correction rates, or how inconsistencies between public transit maps and routing APIs are resolved. This weakens confidence in label reliability.

The dataset’s legal and reproducibility status is unclear. The paper says maps come from public sources and that the benchmark does not redistribute copyrighted map images, but the visual benchmark depends on those images. It is not clear whether future users can reproduce the exact visual inputs, especially if source maps change or cannot be redistributed.

The “training set” claim is underdeveloped: the paper reserves 312 samples as a test set and the rest as training data for future use, but does not explain intended training protocols, leakage prevention, or whether releasing train data could quickly contaminate model evaluations.

The text-only ablation is limited to a small subset of models and does not fully isolate visual grounding. Since route planning can often be answered from memorized transit knowledge or station names, stronger controls would be needed, such as synthetic renamed maps, station-name perturbations, or map-only/text-only counterfactuals.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. A transit-map benchmark is useful, but the technical contribution is primarily dataset curation plus benchmarking; the evaluation framework is not especially principled, and the empirical insights are weakened by the comparison issues above.

Presentation has several clarity and precision issues, including inconsistent difficulty terminology (“medium” versus “middle”), limited details about image preprocessing per model in the main experiments, and unclear implementation details for API-based closed-source evaluations. These are not merely cosmetic because they affect reproducibility.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and underexplored evaluation gap: fine-grained visual and spatial reasoning over dense, high-resolution transit maps. This is a useful setting because it stresses OCR-like perception, line/color discrimination, topology, transfer consistency, and route planning in a single realistic visual artifact.

REASONMAP is reasonably well motivated and carefully scoped, with 1,008 human-verified QA pairs over 30 cities in 13 countries, multiple languages, difficulty labels, and both short and long route-answer formats. The dataset construction pipeline, including map metadata extraction, manual correction, route collection from map services, and filtering of routes not visually traceable on the map, is a meaningful contribution.

The empirical study is broad for a benchmark paper: 15 MLLMs are evaluated, including open-source and closed-source base/reasoning variants. The paper reports both accuracy and a route-quality map score, token counts, difficulty-aware results, city-wise variation, visual-masking ablations, and qualitative error cases.

The findings are interesting and practically relevant. The contrast between open-source reasoning models underperforming their base counterparts while closed-source reasoning models improve, together with the text-only ablation showing partial reliance on prior knowledge, provides useful evidence about current MLLM limitations on high-resolution visual grounding.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes helpful appendices with question templates, evaluation algorithms, map sources, case analyses, high-resolution preprocessing discussion, limitations, and licensing/ethical notes.
weaknesses: The benchmark remains modest in scale and diversity relative to the strength of some claims: only 30 maps and 312 test samples are used for the reported benchmark, with hard questions underrepresented. Some difficulty buckets are extremely small, including one reported bucket with a single sample, making fine-grained difficulty conclusions statistically fragile.

The evaluation metrics need stronger justification and specification. The correctness check mainly verifies endpoint consistency, route-name existence, stop validity, and transfer continuity, but it does not clearly assess route optimality or segment ordering beyond broad feasibility. The map score uses hand-designed weights and bonuses, but its calibration, sensitivity, and agreement with human judgments are not validated.

The difficulty-aware weighting scheme is heuristic. The chosen weights may materially affect model ranking, yet the paper does not appear to report unweighted results, confidence intervals, or robustness of conclusions to alternative weighting choices.

The text-only ablation is valuable but incomplete: it is run on only a subset of models, and the paper sometimes interprets performance drops as evidence of visual grounding without fully separating visual perception from memorized transit knowledge, language/city familiarity, and prompt-format effects.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully established from the manuscript alone. The paper states code/toolkit release and lists sources, but the dataset apparently does not redistribute copyrighted map images, and closed-source model APIs/default settings may change over time. More detail on exact prompts, parsing rules, image preprocessing/resizing, API dates, and released metadata would be needed for reliable replication.

Some claims about why reasoning variants succeed or fail are plausible but speculative. Explanations involving RL-induced output-distribution bias, broader knowledge coverage, or visual integration are not directly tested, so these should be framed more cautiously as hypotheses supported by observed trends rather than causal conclusions.

strengths: The paper targets a clear and underexplored capability: fine-grained visual grounding plus spatial/path reasoning over dense high-resolution transit maps. This is a meaningful complement to existing VQA, visual reasoning, and map-understanding benchmarks, many of which either use coarser map tasks or synthetic/abstract visual reasoning.

The dataset construction is reasonably well motivated: 30 cities across 13 countries, multilingual maps, high average resolution, manually corrected metro data, human verification, map/question difficulty labels, and both short and long route-answer formats. The task is concrete and easy to understand.

The evaluation is more informative than simple exact-match QA. Separating route feasibility/correctness from a graded map score for route quality, via-stop count, and via-stop enumeration is useful for diagnosing partial success.

The empirical study is broad for a benchmark paper, covering 16 MLLMs, open- and closed-source models, base and reasoning variants, visual-masking experiments, symbolic-map experiments, language-prior ablations, difficulty/city breakdowns, and case analyses.

The results reveal interesting and actionable observations: current MLLMs perform poorly in absolute terms, visual input matters for stronger models, open-source reasoning-tuned models can underperform base models on this setting, and failures often arise from grounding and spatial planning rather than OCR alone.
The GRPO fine-tuning baseline, while not the main contribution, provides a useful starting point and shows that the benchmark can drive measurable improvements under cross-city evaluation.
weaknesses: The benchmark is relatively small: 1,008 total QA pairs and only 312 test samples. Some difficulty buckets are very sparse, including a bucket with a single sample, which weakens fine-grained claims about difficulty trends and weighted performance robustness.

The correctness metric appears to check endpoint consistency, route-name existence, valid stops on each line, and transfer consistency, but it does not fully establish optimality or path validity at the level implied by the questions. A response can be marked correct as a feasible route while quality/optimality is deferred to the map score, so the meaning of “accuracy” should be interpreted cautiously.

Ground truth depends partly on Google/Gaode route services and selected reference routes. Even with manual filtering, transit APIs may encode service assumptions, route preferences, or temporal availability not visible in a static map; the paper does not fully characterize ambiguity, alternative optimal routes, or inter-annotator agreement for route validity.

Reproducibility has some unresolved risk. The paper states that map images are from public sources and that copyrighted map images are not redistributed, yet the benchmark depends on those exact high-resolution maps. If only links or derived annotations are released, link rot, licensing restrictions, and map-version changes could make exact reproduction difficult.

The dataset construction details are still somewhat underspecified for a benchmark paper: sampling of stop pairs, manual correction protocol, expert qualifications, post-correction error estimates, train/test city split criteria, and exact API query settings/timestamps are not described enough to independently audit the data.

The weighting scheme for difficulty-aware accuracy is hand-designed and only lightly justified. Since headline results are weighted, additional reporting of unweighted accuracy and confidence intervals would be important, especially with the small and imbalanced hard subset.

The RL baseline improvements are encouraging but limited to Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B and modest absolute performance. The paper argues SFT is insufficient because the metric is non-differentiable, but does not compare against supervised fine-tuning on the same training set, leaving the training conclusion under-supported.

Several conclusions about base versus reasoning models are plausible but somewhat overinterpreted. Closed-source comparisons are not controlled, and differences may reflect model scale, image preprocessing, hidden prompting, training data, or API behavior rather than reasoning tuning per se.

The task domain is narrow: transit maps are a useful structured visual artifact, but the paper’s broader claims about fine-grained visual reasoning should be framed as evidence within this domain rather than as general conclusions about spatial reasoning.

Presentation is generally clear, but some algorithms and score definitions are hard to parse, and the paper would benefit from more precise metric notation, clearer release/licensing statements, and more transparent examples of ambiguous or rejected ground-truth cases.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant gap: fine-grained visual and spatial reasoning over dense transit maps is a meaningful stress test for MLLMs, and the task is more visually grounded than many text-heavy multimodal benchmarks.

The benchmark includes several useful ingredients: high-resolution maps from multiple cities, short and long question formats, manual checking, a rule-based evaluator, experiments on 16 models, visual-masking analysis, and a small RL fine-tuning baseline.
The empirical results are potentially interesting, especially the low absolute performance of strong models and the observation that visual input removal hurts many closed-source systems.
weaknesses: The evidential basis is too thin for the main claims. The benchmark has only 1,008 QA pairs and the reported test set has 312 samples, with highly uneven difficulty buckets; the appendix notes one bucket has only a single sample, making difficulty-wise conclusions unreliable.

The dataset construction and ground truth are not sufficiently auditable. Reference routes are obtained from Google/Gaode and filtered manually, but the criteria for optimality, alternative valid routes, API settings, temporal dependence, and disagreement resolution are not detailed enough. The reported 16% error rate found by domain experts also raises concern about annotation reliability.

The evaluation metric is ad hoc and under-justified. The map score uses hand-set point values, caps, bonuses, and difficulty weights, but there is little validation that it correlates with human judgments of route quality. The strict output format also makes some measured failures partly instruction-following/parser failures rather than visual reasoning failures.

Reproducibility is weak for a benchmark paper. The manuscript says copyrighted maps are not redistributed, the map-source table appears as placeholder links in the appendix, closed-source APIs are evaluated with default settings, and important preprocessing/evaluation normalization details are only described qualitatively.

Several conclusions are overclaimed. The open-source base vs reasoning and closed-source reasoning-vs-base comparisons involve heterogeneous model families, sizes, APIs, and image pipelines, without statistical significance tests or controls sufficient to support a general claim about reasoning tuning.

The RL baseline is not convincing as a contribution. It is run only on two Qwen models, lacks comparison to supervised fine-tuning or format-only training, uses a small training set, and optimizes accuracy/format rather than the full proposed quality metric; improvements may reflect format adaptation or dataset memorization rather than better visual reasoning.

The visual-masking, language, symbolic-representation, and error analyses are suggestive but shallow. Some models improve without images, language experiments are limited to two Chinese cities with manual aliases, and the symbolic baseline does not establish a principled ceiling or isolate perception from planning rigorously.
Overall, the paper has a worthwhile benchmark idea, but the current manuscript does not yet provide enough rigor, validation, or reproducibility for acceptance at CVPR.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful and under-tested capability gap: fine-grained visual grounding plus spatial route reasoning over dense, high-resolution transit maps. This is a useful complement to existing VQA, math-reasoning, and coarse map benchmarks.

REASONMAP is reasonably well scoped and practically motivated, with 1,008 human-verified QA pairs from 30 cities in 13 countries, multilingual station names, difficulty labels, short/long question variants, and train/test splits across disjoint cities.

The evaluation is more informative than a single exact-match score. The paper separates route validity/correctness from a graded map score, and the appendix provides algorithmic details, component-wise error analysis, and sensitivity checks for the scoring design.

The benchmark results are broad and interesting: 16 MLLMs are evaluated, including open-source/base/reasoning and closed-source models. The finding that open-source reasoning-tuned models underperform base variants on this visual-spatial task is noteworthy and supported by quantitative results and case studies.

The visual-masking and symbolic-map experiments strengthen the central claim that successful performance requires more than language priors, while also clarifying how much difficulty comes from visual grounding versus route reasoning.

The GRPO fine-tuning baseline is a useful addition. Even though it is limited in scope, it demonstrates that the proposed training split and reward signals can improve performance under a cross-city setting.
weaknesses: The benchmark is still fairly small for drawing strong general conclusions: the main test set has only 312 samples, and some difficulty/city buckets are tiny, including a reported hard-middle bucket with only one sample. This makes fine-grained claims about difficulty, cities, and scaling trends statistically fragile.

The notion of an 'optimal route' is not fully pinned down. Reference routes are obtained from Google/Gaode APIs and then filtered for visual traceability, but transit-map optimality can depend on time, service schedules, walking constraints, map-service preferences, and whether visually valid alternatives are accepted. The metric takes the best over collected references, but may still penalize valid routes not returned by the APIs.

The correctness metric checks route/station validity and transfer consistency, but it does not appear to enforce global optimality or shortest/least-transfer route validity except indirectly through the reference-based map score. This creates a mismatch with prompts asking for one optimal route.

The difficulty-aware weighting is hand-designed and somewhat arbitrary. Although the weights are moderate, the paper would be stronger with unweighted confidence intervals or significance tests, especially because headline rankings and model comparisons are based on a small weighted test set.

The comparison between base and reasoning models is suggestive but not fully controlled. Reasoning models differ in architecture, training data, image preprocessing, token budgets, and API behavior; the paper acknowledges some closed-source unfairness, but the central open-vs-closed reasoning conclusion should be stated more cautiously.

High-resolution image handling is a major confound. Different models use different resizing, tiling, token compression, and positional encoding strategies, and API models may process images differently from open-source models. This affects whether failures reflect reasoning ability or input preprocessing limitations.

Dataset construction relies partly on MLLM extraction plus manual correction, but the paper gives limited annotation protocol detail: no inter-annotator agreement, no sample of corrected errors, no audit after the reported 16% initial error rate, and limited discussion of translation/alias normalization edge cases.

The RL baseline is useful but incomplete as evidence for training methodology. It only covers Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, lacks SFT or rejection-sampling baselines, and uses rewards close to the evaluation metric, so the gains mainly establish metric optimization rather than broader reasoning improvement.

Reproducibility is promising but not fully demonstrated in the manuscript. Code and dataset release are stated, yet map images may not be redistributed due to licensing, and exact API versions, closed-source model snapshots, parsing rules, and map-service route responses may be hard to reproduce exactly.

The writing is generally clear, but some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially around scaling laws, the causes of open-source reasoning model failures, and the principal capability gap between open- and closed-source models. These should be framed as observed trends on REASONMAP rather than broad conclusions.
